This document says exactly what the gateway speaks, exactly how far each driver
has been verified, and what to do about everything else. It is the first thing
to read and the one to trust when something disagrees with it.

The list of native protocols is derived from the drivers compiled into the
binary, `/api/protocols`, the Protocols screen and the MCP `describe_protocol`
tool all read the same registry. The catalog cannot advertise a protocol the
binary does not have.

## Verification status

Honesty about this is the whole point of the document, so it comes before the
detail.

| Protocol | Native | Verified against | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Modbus TCP/RTU | yes | a real Modbus server, in-process, over TCP | **verified live** |
| OPC UA | yes | Microsoft opc-plc (.NET) and Emberburn (Python), anonymous and unsecured; HotLoop's own OPC UA server and opc-plc, for user name and password, Sign and SignAndEncrypt; **Ignition 8.3.9**, Basic256Sha256 SignAndEncrypt with a user name | **verified live against Ignition 8.3.9 and two other independent servers; NOT verified against KEPServerEX, WinCC, Siemens or Beckhoff** |
| MQTT / Sparkplug B | yes | Eclipse Mosquitto 2.0 with crafted Tahu frames | **verified live** |
| MTConnect | yes | golden agent documents, served over HTTP | **verified live** |
| HTTP / REST | yes | real HTTP endpoints | **verified live** |
| S7comm | yes | frame-level decode and encode tests | **NOT verified against hardware** |
| EtherNet/IP | yes | address, batching and type-mapping tests | **NOT verified against hardware** |
| UniFi Network | yes | a real UniFi Network Application (10.6) with emulated switches and a gateway adopted over the real inform protocol, logged in as a View Only account; a real UniFi OS Server (5.1, Network 10.6) for the UniFi OS login ; read-only against the house Cloud Gateway Ultra and Express 7 (Network 10.6.106) with real USW-Lite-8-PoE switches and a U5G Backup | **verified live, read-only, on real consoles and switches, WAN and failover included. PoE draw above zero not seen yet**, see [UNIFI.md](/iot/unifi/#on-real-gear-2026-09-28) |

**S7comm and EtherNet/IP have not been run against a physical PLC.** Their
decoding is tested thoroughly, every data type, sign extension, the two-byte S7
STRING header, byte ordering, block planning, read-modify-write for bits, but
tested decoding is not the same as a value that came off a real controller. If
you are the first person to point either at real hardware, treat it as
commissioning and check a known value before trusting a screen.

Everything else in this table has moved real values off a real server.

**OPC UA with a user name and password, over a secured channel, is verified
against Ignition 8.3.9**, the current stable release, in both directions: the
driver reading Ignition's server, and Ignition's client reading the Gateway's own
OPC UA server. Setup notes, and the bugs Ignition flushed out, are under
[Ignition 8.3](#ignition-83). It is also tested
against HotLoop's own OPC UA server (built on a different library from the
driver, `awcullen/opcua` against `gopcua`) and Microsoft's opc-plc. None of that
is KEPServerEX, WinCC, a Siemens controller, or a Beckhoff one, and each of those
has its own defaults and its own habits about certificates and token policies.
Treat the first connection to any of them as commissioning. What was
tested, and the one policy that failed against a server, is under
[OPC UA: security and credentials](#opc-ua-security-and-credentials).

## Native protocols

### OPC UA

Prefer this one when a device offers a choice. It browses, it is properly
secured, and it subscribes.

The driver **subscribes rather than polls**. The server sends a value when it
changes, at a rate it can sustain, instead of being asked the same question
every scan by a client with no idea whether anything moved. If a server refuses
a subscription the driver falls back to batched reads rather than failing the
device.

It also falls back when a subscription delivers nothing at all. A server sends
every node's current value in its first publish and never again until it
changes, so a lost first publish means a setpoint that reads bad for as long as
the session lasts. If ten publishing intervals pass (five seconds at least) with
no value from the subscription, the driver logs a warning, deletes the
subscription and reads the tags on every poll until the device next reconnects.
The OPC UA client library this driver is built on can start its publish loop
paused on a loaded host and never send a publish request; that is the case this
exists for.

**Address the nodes by namespace URI.** This matters more than it looks:

```
nsu=http://opcua.edge.server;s=Zone1_Temperature    good
ns=3;s=Zone1_Temperature                            works until it doesn't
```

A namespace *index* is assigned in whatever order the server happens to load its
namespaces. Add a namespace, upgrade firmware, and index 3 quietly becomes
something else, every reading is then wrong with no error anywhere. The URI is
part of the model and does not move. `Browse` returns the URI form for exactly
this reason.

A bare string is rejected as an address. gopcua would happily read `Temperature`
as `ns=0;s=Temperature`, which means a typo parses cleanly into a node that does
not exist and the tag reads bad forever. An explicit form is required so the
mistake surfaces when you save it.

**Discover tags declares each tag as the type the server says the node holds**:
Boolean is `bool`, the integer types keep their width (`int16`, `uint16`,
`int32`, `uint32`, `int64`, `uint64`; SByte and Byte take the next size up),
Float and Double are `float`, and String, DateTime, LocalizedText and the other
types the driver reads as text are `string`. A type the server will not say, or
one with no better name (an enumeration, a structure), stays `float`. Until the
Ignition work below, every discovered tag was `float`. The driver still read a
String node's text, but the tag said float, and the Gateway's own OPC UA server
publishes a tag as the type it is declared, so a client of that server got
`Bad_TypeMismatch` for it. Ignition showed Emberburn's `System_Status` exactly
that way. Tags imported before the fix keep their type: change a text tag to
`string` by hand.

Configuration: the security, identity and certificate options are described under
[OPC UA: security and credentials](#opc-ua-security-and-credentials). The rest
are `subscribe`, `publishIntervalMs`, `samplingIntervalMs`, `queueSize`,
`sessionTimeoutMs`, `browseMaxNodes`, `browseRoot`, and `browseServerNodes`. An
option name the driver does not know is an error that lists the ones it does,
not a setting that is silently ignored: a typo in `securityMode` would
otherwise connect with no security at all and look exactly like a working
device.

**Discover tags leaves out the server's own `Server` object** (`i=2253`: its
status, capabilities, diagnostics, namespace array and configuration). Every
OPC UA server has one, and on opc-plc it was hundreds of variables
mixed in with the plant's own. Set `browseServerNodes` to `true` on
the device to get them back, or set `browseRoot` to `i=2253` to look inside it
on purpose; a browse that starts there still walks it.

### OPC UA: security and credentials

Until 4.15.0 the driver could only make an anonymous, unsecured connection, and
not to any server that follows the specification: it never asked the server which
identity token policies it offered, so it sent an empty token policy id, which a
compliant server refuses. That included HotLoop's own OPC UA server. The driver
now discovers the server's endpoints, picks one that matches the device, and
echoes the policy id that endpoint listed.

#### Device options

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `securityMode` | `None` | `None`, `Sign`, or `SignAndEncrypt`. Left out with a `securityPolicy` other than `None`, it is `SignAndEncrypt`. |
| `securityPolicy` | the best the server offers for the mode | `None`, `Basic256Sha256`, `Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep`, or `Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss`. `Basic128Rsa15` and `Basic256` are refused. |
| `username`, `password` | anonymous | User name authentication. |
| `allowInsecureCredentials` | `false` | Allows a password to be sent over an unsecured channel (`securityMode` `None`), or when nothing encrypts it. |
| `certFile`, `keyFile` | generated | This client's application certificate and its RSA key, for a secured mode. Set both or neither. |
| `pkiDir` | `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_CLIENT_PKI_DIR` (`/data/opcua-client-pki`) | Where the generated certificate and the `trusted/` and `rejected/` stores live. |
| `serverCertThumbprints` | none | SHA-1 (40 hex digits) or SHA-256 (64) thumbprints of server certificates to trust without a file in `trusted/`. Colons and spaces are ignored. |
| `insecureSkipVerify` | `false` | Accept any server certificate. |

A device with none of these set is what it always was: anonymous, over an
unsecured channel. That is unchanged, and the tests against opc-plc that
predate this work still pass unmodified.

#### How the driver picks an endpoint

The driver asks the server for its endpoints over an unsecured channel, which
the specification requires servers to allow for discovery and which carries
nothing secret, since the endpoint list is public by design. It keeps the
endpoints whose security mode and policy match the device, and among those the
token policy for the device's identity (anonymous, or user name when a `username`
is set). The identity token it then sends carries the policy id that endpoint
listed; it never sends an empty one.

- **It never selects `Basic128Rsa15` or `Basic256`.** Both are deprecated by the
  OPC Foundation. This holds when one has the highest security level on the list,
  which is how servers rank them, and when one is the only thing the server
  offers, in which case the connection fails with an error that says so. A device
  cannot be configured to use one, and a token policy that would encrypt a
  password with one is refused as well. HotLoop's own server offers both
  alongside the modern policies and cannot turn them off, so this is exercised
  against a real server, and the tests check that neither policy's URI appears in
  what the driver sends.
- **When the device names no policy it prefers `Basic256Sha256`, then
  `Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep`, then `Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss`**, whatever security level
  the server gives them. The order is by how widely each works, not by strength.
  Against opc-plc, `Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss` fails: the library the driver is built
  on cannot open a channel with it, and the connection is closed with nothing to
  say why. A bare `gopcua` client with none of this driver's code fails the same
  way, and the policy works against HotLoop's own server. It is used only when a
  device names it.
- **If nothing matches, the error lists what the server does offer**, with the
  policy and token policy id of each endpoint, so the configuration can be fixed
  from the message alone.

#### The client's own certificate

Any secured mode needs an application certificate. If the device names a
`certFile` and `keyFile` they are used as they stand, after checks (RSA, at
least 2048 bits, not expired). Otherwise a self-signed one is generated on first
use and kept in the PKI directory: RSA-2048, five years, the application URI
`urn:hotloop:client:<host name>` in the subject alternative names, the key at
mode `0600`, the certificate at `0644`, and the directories at `0750`. The layout
mirrors the OPC UA server's:

```
own/cert.pem, own/key.pem   this client's certificate
trusted/                    server certificates an operator has approved
rejected/                   server certificates the driver turned away
```

It is not regenerated on a routine start, so a server that has been told to trust
it is not told again. It is replaced, with a warning that every server must
approve the new one, only if it cannot be read, is not RSA of at least 2048 bits,
or has under 30 days left. Devices that start at the same moment share one
certificate rather than each writing their own.

The directory must be writable and persistent. In the Helm chart that is
`opcuaClient.persistence.enabled` (off by default, because it adds a volume to an
existing install); on the edge relay it is the existing `/data` volume. Without a
writable directory a secured device reports an error that names the variable to
set, rather than connecting with certificates that would be lost at the next
restart.

The **server** must also trust this certificate, which is the server's own
setting. For HotLoop's own server that is the same move: the driver's certificate
appears in the server's `rejected/` directory after the first refused attempt,
and moving it to `trusted/` approves it. When a server closes the connection
while the secure channel is opening, which is how many servers turn away a
certificate they do not trust, the error names this client's certificate file and
thumbprint so the operator knows what to look for on the server.

#### Approving a server's certificate

For a secured mode, or for a password that is to be encrypted to the server's
key, **the driver does not accept whatever certificate the server presents.** It
trusts the certificate only if it is pinned in the device's
`serverCertThumbprints` or is the exact certificate in `trusted/`. Anything else
is written to `rejected/<thumbprint>.der` and the connection fails, before any
credential is sent, with a message like:

```
opcua: the server at opc.tcp://plc-01:4840 presented a certificate that is not
trusted (subject "CN=PLC01", SHA-1 thumbprint 5A6DB35A..., expires 2031-09-18).
It has been saved to /data/opcua-client-pki/rejected/5A6DB35A....der. To approve
it, first check that the thumbprint matches the one the server shows, then move
that file into /data/opcua-client-pki/trusted (the next connection attempt picks
it up; no restart is needed). Alternatively pin it by adding the thumbprint to
this device's serverCertThumbprints. Until then this device will not connect
```

Check the thumbprint against the server's own display before approving: that
comparison is the whole of the trust decision. Then `mv` the file into `trusted/`
(PEM and DER files are both read), and the device connects on its next attempt,
which is within the runtime's reconnect interval. Some details:

- Trust is by the exact certificate, not by a chain. A server whose certificate
  is issued by a CA is approved by placing that server's own certificate in
  `trusted/`, the same as a self-signed one. Trusting a CA is not supported.
- A certificate that has expired but was approved by an operator is still
  trusted, with a warning in the log on each connect. Refusing one an operator
  approved on purpose would only push them toward `insecureSkipVerify`.
- A file in `trusted/` that is not a certificate is skipped and reported, and
  does not make the other approved servers unreachable.
- `rejected/` holds at most 256 files, so a server that presents a different
  certificate on every connection cannot fill the disk. Past that the connection
  is still refused, and the message says the file was not kept and how to approve
  the certificate anyway.
- `insecureSkipVerify` turns the check off. A party in the path can then
  impersonate the server, and read what is sent to it, including the password.
  It is off by default and warns, with the certificate's thumbprint, on every
  connect.

An anonymous device on an unsecured channel needs none of this, because nothing
is signed or encrypted to the server's key.

#### Credentials

A password is refused, before it is sent, unless the channel is secured and
something encrypts the password. What the driver decides, from what the server
offers for the endpoint it matched:

| Channel | The server's user name token policy | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `SignAndEncrypt` | encrypts the password (the usual case) | connects |
| `SignAndEncrypt` | does not | connects: the encrypted channel carries it, and the log says so |
| `Sign` | encrypts the password | connects |
| `Sign` | does not | **refused** unless `allowInsecureCredentials`. `Sign` authenticates messages but does not hide them. |
| `None` | encrypts the password | **refused** unless `allowInsecureCredentials`. On an unsecured channel the key the password is encrypted to comes from a reply nothing authenticates, so anyone who can alter traffic can recover it. With the opt-in it connects, with a warning. |
| `None` | does not | **refused** unless `allowInsecureCredentials` |

**A user name over `securityMode` `None` is refused even when the server's token
policy encrypts the password.** Encryption whose key an attacker can choose is not
protection against that attacker, and on an unsecured channel the certificate the
password is encrypted to is taken from the server's reply to `CreateSession`,
which nothing authenticates (the test below substitutes a certificate and
recovers the password). The error says this and names the fix, `securityMode`
`SignAndEncrypt`. Anonymous sessions are not affected.

`allowInsecureCredentials` is the one switch that lets a password go out on
those terms. It is off by default and warns on every connect when it is what
allowed the connection. Where the token policy encrypts the password it changes
what a listener can read, not what a party that alters traffic can: see
[what crosses the network](#what-crosses-the-network). Even with it, the server's
certificate must be approved first when the password is encrypted to it.

The password is a secret everywhere the driver and the API handle it:

- **API responses.** It is replaced by `[redacted]` in every response that returns
  a device (`GET /api/devices`, `GET /api/devices/{id}`, and the response to a
  save), so a viewer, who holds `devices.read`, cannot read it. As of 4.15.1 this
  holds for every role, admin included, and for the credentials of every protocol,
  not only this one. Saving a device back with the placeholder keeps the stored
  password; a new value replaces it; an empty string clears it; the placeholder for
  a device with no password is refused rather than stored. Leaving the field out
  now keeps it (in 4.15.0 it cleared it). The full rules are in
  [AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/#device-credentials-are-write-only). The web UI's device
  editor shows the configuration as the API returns it and saves what it shows,
  which this handles, so editing a device does not lose its password. (The tests
  exercise that through the API, not through a browser.)
- **Logs and errors.** Neither the driver's log lines nor any error it returns
  carries the password: the messages are built from status codes and the device's
  non-secret settings. The tests capture the process log, the server's log, and
  the errors, and search all of them for the password.
- **MCP tools and resources, the live event stream, the system log.** None returns a
  device's configuration (each describes a device through a fixed set of fields),
  and tests call every tool and resource, open the stream, and read the system log
  with a password configured, and find it nowhere.
- **The database and backups.** The password is stored in the device's `config`
  column as the other drivers' are. Up to 4.16.0 that's in the clear, and a backup
  contains it. From 4.17.0 it's encrypted with a key kept outside the database (see
  "Encrypted at rest" below), so a dump or a backup holds ciphertext. Either way,
  see [BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/#protect-the-backup-files) and protect the database
  and the backup volume accordingly.
- **The edge relay.** A device file carries the password too. In the Helm chart, put
  a device file with credentials in a Secret and name it in `devicesSecret`;
  devices set directly in the chart's values end up in a ConfigMap. A device file
  pushed through fleet config push is published, retained, to an MQTT topic, so
  the broker must carry TLS and restrict who may read that topic.

A wrong password is a clear error, in one attempt, with no hang and no retry
inside the driver:

```
opcua: authentication rejected: the server at opc.tcp://plc-01:4840 rejected the
user name and password for "svc-hotloop" (StatusBadUserAccessDenied). ...
```

The runtime then waits **ten minutes** (jittered to between five and ten) before
the next attempt, instead of climbing through its usual reconnect backoff
(`HOTLOOP_RECONNECT_MAX`, 60 seconds by default). Two things make a refused login
more expensive to repeat than a network fault. A server that locks an account
after a few failures turns every quick retry into an outage for whoever else uses
that account. And each refused login can leave a **session that was created and
never activated** on the server, which counts against its session limit until it
times out (the library asks for twenty minutes; `sessionTimeoutMs` changes it):
against HotLoop's own server, a device with a wrong password retrying every few
seconds filled its default limit of twenty sessions, after which the server
refused every other client with `BadTooManySessions`. A controller with a small
session table is more exposed than that. The device does not stop retrying, so a
server whose password is fixed on its side recovers within ten minutes without
anyone touching HotLoop; correcting the password on the device, or switching it
off and on, starts a new worker, which tries at once.

#### What crosses the network

Measured, not reasoned: the tests put a recording proxy between the driver and a
server and search every byte in both directions. The search finds bytes known to
be there (the server's endpoint list, sent in the clear), which is what shows the
proxy recorded the conversation.

| Configuration | Password | User name | Tag node ids and values |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SignAndEncrypt` | not visible | not visible | not visible |
| `Sign` | not visible (the token policy encrypts it) | **readable** | **readable** |
| `None`, user name, server's token policy encrypts (needs `allowInsecureCredentials`) | not visible | **readable** | **readable** |
| `None`, anonymous | not applicable | not applicable | **readable** |
| a server that offers an unencrypted password, with `allowInsecureCredentials` | **readable** | **readable** | depends on the mode |

The last row is tested against a server that does not really offer that: a party
in front of a real server rewrites its endpoint list to say the password is
unencrypted, on the channel discovery uses, which nothing authenticates. That is
also how the tests show the refusal: without the opt-in the driver refuses, opens
only the discovery connection, and no credential is on the wire. The endpoint list
is exactly the thing a party in the path can rewrite, which is why the driver's
rule is applied to what it is told and not left to the server to enforce.

An unsecured channel with a password has a limit the table does not show, and a
test does; it is why the driver refuses that combination without the opt-in. The
password is encrypted to the server's certificate, which keeps it
from a listener, and the driver will not send it until that certificate is
approved. But the certificate the OPC UA library encrypts to is the one in the
server's reply when the session is created, and on an unsecured channel that
reply is not authenticated. A party that can alter traffic puts its own
certificate in it, and the password is then encrypted to that party's key: the
test does this, decrypts the password with the substituted key, and gets it back.
**Over `Sign` or `SignAndEncrypt` the same party cannot**, because the reply is
protected by keys it does not have. Without `allowInsecureCredentials` the driver
refuses to send the password at all, and the test shows the same party then gets
nothing; with it, the driver warns on every connect. Use `SignAndEncrypt`
wherever the server offers it; an unsecured channel with a password, opted in, is
protection against a listener and nothing more.

#### Reconnection

The OPC UA library's own reconnect is switched off, and the runtime reconnects.
The library, once a session is lost, opens a new one with the credentials it was
given and, when the server refuses them, tries again straight away with no delay:
about twenty refused logins in twelve seconds was measured, against a server
whose password had been changed. That is how an account gets locked out for
everyone who shares it. Now a lost session makes `Poll` report an error, the
runtime's worker closes the driver and opens a new one, and the new one discovers
the endpoints, checks the server's certificate, and signs in again, with the
runtime's jittered backoff and the ten-minute wait after an authentication
failure. A restart of the server is survived the same way: the device reads the
new value after the restart, having signed in again, which the tests check by
counting the server's logins and by changing the value after the restart.

A device with no tags has nothing to read, and until 4.15.2 that meant its poll
sent nothing at all. The server closed the idle session after its session timeout,
the device kept saying connected because nobody had asked the server anything,
and every browse failed with `BadSessionIDInvalid` until the process restarted.
That is every device at the exact moment somebody adds it and clicks Discover
tags. Ignition caught it. Now a device with no tags reads the server's state on
every poll, which keeps the session alive and notices when it dies, and a browse
that finds the session gone reports it so the runtime reconnects.

A tag that has not changed since before the session began now reads its current
value with good quality. Before, the placeholder reading reported while waiting
for the first value was newer than the value's own source timestamp, and the
runtime keeps the newest reading and discarded the value, so a stable tag read bad
until it next changed.

#### What was tested, and what was not

**Tested**, against HotLoop's own OPC UA server, with a real database, real
users, and real bcrypt hashes, and against Microsoft's opc-plc:

- anonymous and user name and password over `None`, `Sign` and `SignAndEncrypt`,
  with `Basic256Sha256`, `Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep`, and (against HotLoop's server
  only) `Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss`;
- the operator's whole journey: a server certificate refused and saved, approved
  by moving it, then the server refusing the driver's certificate and the message
  that says so, then both approved and a value read;
- a wrong password, an unknown server certificate, a user name over `None`
  refused without `allowInsecureCredentials` and, with it, refused until the
  server's certificate is approved and then connecting, a deprecated policy named
  and left to be chosen, and the credential rules above against a rewritten
  endpoint list;
- a restart of the server, a password that stops working after the device has
  connected, and a stable tag, each through the runtime's worker and a second
  HotLoop instance;
- a device with no tags left idle past the server's session timeout, then
  browsed, and the same device after the server restarts under it;
- Ignition 8.3.9, below;
- the anonymous tests that predate this work, against opc-plc, unchanged, and the
  Emberburn interop tests against a python-opcua (freeopcua) server standing in
  for Emberburn, which is built on that library. Emberburn itself was not
  available for this change, so the path through the new endpoint selection has
  not been run against it;
- the password absent from API output, the live event stream, the system log,
  MCP output, the driver's log, the server's log, and every error string;
- `go test -race -count=10` on the driver and OPC UA server packages.

**Not verified.** KEPServerEX, WinCC, Siemens, Beckhoff and any other
production server except Ignition, and Ignition only as far as the next section
says. Each may behave differently about which policies it offers and
how it turns away a certificate. Also not tested or not supported:

- A change in behavior for existing devices, in the few cases it applies. Every
  connect now asks the server for its endpoints first, and a device with no
  security options needs an unsecured endpoint that lists an anonymous token
  policy with an id. A server that accepted anonymous sessions without listing
  one, which worked before only because it was not checking, is now refused with
  an error that lists what it offers.
- X.509 certificate and issued-token user authentication. Before 4.15.0 a device
  with `certFile` tried to use it as a user certificate and could not work; it is
  now the application certificate, and user certificate authentication is not
  implemented.
- A silently dead connection, one where the network path drops without either end
  seeing it close. The library treats a timed-out publish request as nothing to
  act on, so a device on such a link keeps its last values, and the runtime is not
  told the session is gone, until the operating system gives up on the connection.
  This was already true with the library's own reconnect on; it is listed here
  because the runtime now owns reconnection and depends on the session state to
  know when to.
- Trusting a certificate authority, and certificate revocation. Trust is by exact
  certificate.
- Elliptic-curve security policies, and servers that refuse discovery on an
  unsecured channel.
- `Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss` against a server other than HotLoop's own, where it
  failed, as above.
- Whether a server's own password limits apply: HotLoop's own server, for one,
  cannot log in a user whose password is longer than 64 bytes over OPC UA (the
  library refuses it, see [OPCUA-SERVER.md](/edge/opc-ua-server/)).

#### Ignition 8.3

Verified against **Ignition 8.3.9**, the current stable release, in Inductive
Automation's own container image: HotLoop's driver as the client, Ignition's OPC
UA server on the other end, `Basic256Sha256` with `SignAndEncrypt`, signed in
with a user name and password. Browse found Ignition's tags under
`nsu=urn:inductiveautomation:ignition:opcua:tags`, and the `[System]/Gateway`
clock, CPU, memory and uptime tags imported and read with good quality, pushed
by subscription.

A stock 8.3 gateway will stop you four times before HotLoop gets a word in:

1. **Its OPC UA server listens on localhost only.** Out of the box, 8.3 binds
   port 62541 to `localhost`, so a HotLoop anywhere else gets connection refused
   and nothing else. In the Gateway, under the OPC UA server settings, set Bind
   Addresses to `0.0.0.0`. We also added the host name HotLoop dials to
   Endpoint Addresses; whether the driver needs that was not tested.
2. **Tags are not on OPC UA by default.** Turn on Expose Tag Providers, or all a
   browse finds is the server's own diagnostics and the device folders.
3. **Certificates, both ways.** HotLoop refuses Ignition's certificate until you
   approve it, as above. Ignition refuses HotLoop's until you trust it in the
   Gateway's OPC UA server certificates. On disk that is moving it from
   `data/config/local/com.inductiveautomation.opcua/server/security/pki/rejected/certs`
   to `.../trusted/certs`, no restart. **Ignition does not name that file by the
   SHA-1 thumbprint HotLoop logs.** Open the certificate and compare its
   fingerprint; the file name will not match and that is not a sign of an
   impostor.
4. **The OPC UA login is `opcuauser` / `password`** in the `opcua-module` user
   source, on every fresh install. Change it before anything real connects.

Only what 8.3's server offers out of the box was exercised in this direction:
`Basic256Sha256` and `SignAndEncrypt`.

**The other direction is verified too: Ignition 8.3.9's OPC UA client reads
HotLoop's OPC UA server**, signed in as a HotLoop viewer, over every security
policy and mode Ignition offers. The setup, the certificate trust in both
directions, the gotchas and the policy matrix are in
[OPCUA-SERVER.md](/edge/opc-ua-server/#ignition-83-as-a-client). It found two HotLoop
bugs, both fixed: the server minted a new certificate every time its container
was recreated, which broke Ignition's trust after every upgrade, and Discover
tags declared every tag a float, so a text tag reached Ignition as
`Bad_TypeMismatch` (above). `test/ignition/lab.py` repeats the whole
verification against a running HotLoop and prints PASS or FAIL.

HotLoop's Sparkplug edge node and Edge Relay against Ignition's MQTT Engine are
next and not done.

### Modbus TCP/RTU

The 1979 workhorse. PLCs, VFDs, power meters, RTUs, and the fallback of every
gateway that has nothing better.

```
holding:100:float32:CDAB    a float across registers 100-101, word-swapped
holding:40:bit3             bit 3 of register 40
holding:200:string16        16 characters from register 200
input:12:int16              a signed input register
coil:5                      a single coil
```

**Word order** is the setting people get wrong, and a float read with the wrong
order is not obviously wrong on a screen, it is a plausible number that is not
the truth. All four permutations are supported by the names vendor manuals
print: `ABCD`, `CDAB`, `BADC`, `DCBA`. Set a device default with `byteOrder` and
override per tag with the fourth address field.

**Addressing** is raw and zero-based. If your drawings use the traditional
40001-style numbering, set `oneBased: true` and write the numbers from the
drawings. Getting this wrong by one is the oldest Modbus bug there is.

Reads are merged into blocks: adjacent and near-adjacent registers become one
request. `maxGap` controls how many unused registers are worth reading to avoid a
second round trip (default 8), `maxBlock` caps a single request (default 120,
protocol ceiling 125).

Writing a single bit of a holding register is a read-modify-write, because
Modbus has no atomic bit-set there. The other fifteen bits are preserved.

### MQTT and Sparkplug B

Plain MQTT, or Sparkplug B as a **full primary host application**.

Plain topics:
```
mqtt:plant/line1/temperature              a scalar payload
mqtt:plant/line1/state|data.temperature   JSON, extracted by path
mqtt:plant/+/flow                         wildcards work
```

Sparkplug metrics:
```
spb:GroupId|EdgeNodeId|DeviceId|Metric/Name
spb:Plant|Edge1||Node/Uptime               empty device = a node-level metric
```

As a primary host the driver does the things the specification asks for and most
integrations skip:

- Publishes a retained `STATE` birth with a matching will, so edge nodes can see
  the host drop rather than inferring it from a timeout. Sparkplug 3.0 form
  (`spBv1.0/STATE/<host>` carrying JSON) by default; set `legacyState` for the
  pre-3.0 `ONLINE`/`OFFLINE` string.
- Tracks the per-node rolling sequence number and asks a node to rebirth when it
  skips, because a gap means messages were missed and the alias table can no
  longer be trusted.
- Requests rebirth after its own reconnect. A host that was away has no idea
  what changed while it was gone.
- Matches `NDEATH` to `NBIRTH` by `bdSeq`, so a death certificate left over from
  a previous session cannot kill the current one.

Message ordering is enforced. Delivering Sparkplug messages concurrently
reorders them, which makes a healthy node look like it is dropping messages and
provokes a rebirth storm.

### EtherNet/IP (CIP)

Allen-Bradley ControlLogix, CompactLogix and Micro820. Tags have names, so the
controller can be asked what it holds.

```
Temperature                    type from the tag's declared dataType
Speed:dint                     an explicit type wins
Program:MainProgram.Speed      a program-scoped tag, the colon is part of the path
Zones[0].Heater.On:bool        array elements and UDT members
```

CIP is strongly typed and the controller rejects a read whose declared type does
not match, so the type has to come from somewhere. It is taken from the tag's
`dataType`, or from a `:type` suffix which wins. Unknown falls back to `REAL`,
which most process values are.

Reads are batched into multi-service requests, falling back to individual reads
when a batch fails so that one bad tag path does not blind the other nineteen.

### S7comm

Siemens S7-300, 400, 1200 and 1500, over ISO-on-TCP by rack and slot.

```
db1:0:real        a REAL at DB1.DBD0
db1:4:dint        a DINT at DB1.DBD4
db1:8.3:bool      bit 3 of DB1.DBB8
db2:20:string32   a 32-character STRING
m:10:word         merker word MW10
i:0.1:bool        input I0.1
q:2:byte          output byte QB2
```

The type is required for anything wider than a byte. The protocol cannot tell
you whether four bytes are a REAL or a DINT, that is a fact about the PLC
program, not about the wire.

Defaults to rack 0, slot 1 (S7-1200/1500). S7-300/400 are usually slot 2.
`connectType` defaults to 3 (S7 Basic) so the gateway does not occupy the PG
connection slot an engineer wants for TIA Portal.

There is no browse. An S7 CPU does not publish the layout of its data blocks, that lives in the TIA Portal project.

### MTConnect

Read-only machine tool telemetry. There is no command channel in MTConnect, and
this driver does not pretend otherwise.

Address by `dataItemId` or by name; agents are inconsistent about which is
stable, and machine documentation shows one or the other.

Two details that separate a working integration from a plausible one:
`UNAVAILABLE` is the agent explicitly saying it has no reading, it becomes bad
quality, not the text "UNAVAILABLE" and not zero. And a Condition's meaning is
its element name (`Normal`, `Warning`, `Fault`, `Unavailable`), not its
character data, which is usually empty.

`Browse` reads `/probe` and walks the component tree to any depth.

### HTTP / REST

The catch-all, for energy meters, environmental sensors, OEM controllers and the
REST side of a gateway that speaks something proprietary underneath.

```
power.kw                      nested fields
readings[0].value             array indexing
zones[name=Zone1].temp        select an array element by a field value
$.data.temperature            a leading $. is accepted
```

That third form is the one that matters: these APIs love returning an unordered
array of `{name, value}` objects, and indexing by position is a bug waiting for a
firmware update.

One request serves every tag on the device. `Browse` walks the document and
reports every scalar with the path that reaches it.

### UniFi Network

The plant network as a device: one site on one UniFi console, its switches,
every switch port, PoE draw, the WAN links and the site's health, as read-only
tags that create themselves as gear is adopted. One login per console, the
certificate pinned, and the console password encrypted in the database. It
never writes to the console. It also listens to the console's events websocket,
so a switch dropping off is in the logbook when it happens, with polling still
the truth underneath, and the UniFi tab draws the overview, the map, the
faceplates, the clients, the networks and the WiFi. Everything about it is in
[UNIFI.md](/iot/unifi/).

## Everything else: gateway mode

**PROFINET · EtherCAT · HART · BACnet/IP · DNP3 · FINS · MELSEC/SLMP · CANopen ·
FANUC FOCAS**

These are not spoken natively and there is no driver for them. That is a
deliberate choice, not a gap waiting to be filled with a stub.

Sites running these protocols almost always already have a gateway that
re-publishes on OPC UA or Modbus, a PROFINET IO controller with an OPC UA
server, a HART multiplexer with a Modbus map, a BACnet/IP to Modbus bridge.
Point a device at that endpoint and configure it as OPC UA or Modbus.

Writing nine more drivers that each duplicate what a site's existing gateway
already does would add nine more things to get subtly wrong, for protocols where
the equipment is hardest to test against. If a site genuinely has no gateway and
needs one of these natively, that is a real piece of work to schedule, not a
file to add that logs "not implemented".

**There are no placeholder drivers in this tree.** A protocol either has a
working implementation or it is in this section. The previous version of this
product had sixteen protocol files of which fifteen returned
`"not implemented"`, while the catalog advertised all sixteen. A test now
enforces that every protocol the model declares has a driver compiled in, and
vice versa.

## Device credentials

A device's `config` and `address` are where a driver finds what it logs in with.
These are the credentials each protocol reads, and all of them are write-only
through the API (4.15.1): they show as `[redacted]` to every role, a save that
sends the placeholder or leaves the key out keeps the stored value, and a new
string replaces it. The rules, and what does not go through the API, are in
[AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/#device-credentials-are-write-only).

| Protocol | Credentials in the configuration | Credentials in the address |
|---|---|---|
| OPC UA | `password` (with `username`) | none: user information in the address is hidden, and the driver ignores it |
| MQTT / Sparkplug B | `password` (with `username`) | `mqtt://user:pass@host`, which the client uses |
| HTTP / REST | `password` (with `username`, sent as basic auth); every value in `headers` except plain ones such as `Accept` and `Content-Type`, which is where an API key or `Authorization` header goes; `body` and `writeBody` if they mention a credential | `http://user:pass@host` and `?api_key=` style query values, in the address and in `writeUrl` |
| MTConnect | `password` (with `username`); every value in `headers`, with the same exceptions | `http://user:pass@host` and query values |
| UniFi Network | `password` (with `username`). Only ever stored encrypted: without a key (below) the device can't be saved | none: the address is the console's `https://` URL |
| Modbus, S7comm, EtherNet/IP | none | none: user information in the address is hidden, and the driver ignores it |

**Encrypted at rest.** With `HOTLOOP_SECRET_KEY_FILE` set (the chart sets it,
with a key it generates), every credential in the configuration column above is
encrypted in the database with that key, which lives outside the database, so a
dump or a backup holds ciphertext. The rest of HotLoop, and the drivers, never
see the difference. A credential written into a URL (`mqtt://user:pass@host`)
or into free text is hidden from every screen but stays in the clear in the
database; use the `password` option. See
[BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/#device-credentials-and-the-secret-key).

Any other option whose name looks like a credential (it contains `password`,
`token`, `secret`, `apikey`, `authorization`, `private`, `passphrase`, or ends in
`key`, or has a whole word such as `pass`, `pw`, `auth`, `cred`, or `sig`, among
others) is hidden too, whatever protocol it is in, so an option added to a driver
later is hidden until someone decides it should not be. A test walks every
driver's options and fails until each one is on the list of credentials or the
list of options known not to be. See
[AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/#device-credentials-are-write-only) for the full rules.

## Adding a device

1. **Devices → Add device.** Pick the protocol, give it an address.
2. **Discover tags** where the protocol supports it: OPC UA, EtherNet/IP,
   MTConnect, MQTT (after a Sparkplug birth), HTTP. Modbus and S7comm cannot
   enumerate their own points, so declare those from the device documentation.
3. Imported tags are created **read-only**. A point the device happens to expose
   is not a point somebody has decided may be commanded. Mark tags writable one
   at a time, deliberately.
4. Set `scale` and `offset` for raw counts: `engineering = raw × scale + offset`.
   If the instrument sends a code when a channel is dead or out of range, list
   it under [No-data values](#no-data-values) so it reads bad instead of as a
   number.
5. Set a `deadband` on anything noisy. It suppresses historian writes for
   changes too small to matter, and without it a 12-bit sensor jittering in its
   last bit writes a row every scan forever.

## No-data values

A recorder with a burnt-out thermocouple does not go quiet. It keeps answering,
and what it puts in the register is a code: 0x8005 for "undefined", 0x7FFF for
"over range". Read as an int16 with a scale of 0.1, 0x8005 is -3276.3 degrees,
and until I fixed this it came back as **good** quality, went into the
historian as a real temperature and sat there for the alarms to judge. A dead
sensor looked like a cold one.

So a tag can list the raw values that mean "no measurement". Each one has a
reason. When a reading's raw value is on the list, the reading is **bad**, the
reason is on it, and scale and offset never touch it.

```json
{
  "deviceId": "dx-1", "name": "ch01", "address": "input:1:int16",
  "dataType": "float", "unit": "C", "scale": 0.1, "enabled": true,
  "noData": [
    {"raw": "0x7FFF", "reason": "+over"},
    {"raw": "0x8001", "reason": "-over"},
    {"raw": "0x8002", "reason": "skip"},
    {"raw": "0x8004", "reason": "error"},
    {"raw": "0x8005", "reason": "undefined"},
    {"raw": "0x7F7F", "reason": "power fail"},
    {"raw": "0x7FFA", "reason": "burnout up"},
    {"raw": "0x8006", "reason": "burnout down"}
  ]
}
```

Those eight are the Yokogawa DX family's codes, from the DX communication
manual (IM 04L41B01-17E, section 4.3, page 4-35). They are not special to
HotLoop: it is the same field on every tag of every protocol, and the DX list
is just the one that bit us first. Each one is on the tag, so a recorder
channel that really can read 0x7F7F in some other unit keeps it as a reading.

| Field | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|
| `raw` | The device's code, written the way its manual prints it: `"0x8005"` (hex), `"-32763"` or `32773` (decimal). A string or a bare number. Required |
| `reason` | What the reading's quality says. Up to 120 characters. Left out, it reads `raw value 0x8005 means no measurement`, so a reading never goes bad without saying why |

In the tag editor it is the **No-data values** box: one code per line, the code,
a space, the reason.

### Which number you write

For a register-backed Modbus point the code is the integer the device holds,
after the point's byte and word order is applied. That is the same number the
point decodes to, so a manual that says "the instrument returns 8005h" means
exactly `"0x8005"` here.

- **int16 and the other signed types.** `0x8005` and `-32763` are the same
  register, and so is `32773`. Write whichever the manual does; all three match.
  A code that does not fit the type (`0x10000` on an int16) is refused when the
  device connects, because a list that can never match is worse than an error.
  Two spellings of one value on one tag are refused too.
- **uint16 and the other unsigned types.** `0` up to the type's maximum. A
  negative number is refused.
- **int32, uint32, int64, uint64.** The same rules at 32 and 64 bits.
  `0x7FFFFFFF` on an int32 with `CDAB` word order is the value after the words
  are put the right way round, not the order they came off the wire in.
- **float32 and float64.** The code is the register bit pattern, so it has to be
  hex: `0x7FC00000` for a quiet NaN. A decimal is refused, because 32773 as a
  float and 32773 as a bit pattern are different things and I won't guess.
- **Bits, coils, discrete inputs and strings.** No raw number to compare, so
  `noData` on one is refused when the device connects.

The check is on the raw bits, before decode, before scale, before offset.

### Other protocols

Every driver that hands over an already decoded number checks the same list:
S7comm, EtherNet/IP, OPC UA, HTTP and MQTT (including discovered devices).
What they compare is that decoded number, as a whole number, so write it as
the number it is. An S7 INT holding 0x8005 is -32763, so write `-32763`. Hex
here is only another way to write the same number, because a decoded number has
lost its width and can't be read back as a bit pattern. A fractional value
never matches. The list is only worth setting where the device sends codes
like these; most of what MTConnect and UniFi report never does.

### What a sentinel does

- **Quality** is `bad` and the reading carries the reason. It shows on
  `GET /api/values` and the live stream (`reason`), next to the quality on the
  Tags screen, and on the tag's entities as the `quality_reason` attribute.
- **The value** is empty, not zero and not the scaled code. Scale and offset are
  not applied.
- **The historian** records the quality as bad, the same as any other bad
  reading, and its value column holds nothing meaningful. A bucket with no good
  reading shows as a gap on a trend, as it does for any bad reading.
- **Alarms.** A bad reading never trips a value alarm: high, low, equal,
  rate of change all hold their previous state, same as for any bad reading. A
  `bad-quality` alarm on the tag does fire, and its default message carries the
  reason (`dx-1/ch01 bad-quality: undefined`). Use `{reason}` in your own
  message to put it there.
- **The logbook** records the tag's entity going bad, and the reason is the
  entity's `quality_reason` attribute.

### Where it lives

On the tag, saved with it. Through the API it is the `noData` list on
`POST /api/tags` (see [API.md](/iot/api/#post-apitags)), in the editor it is the
box above, and in an Edge Relay it is the same JSON in the device file's tag
(see [EDGE-RELAY.md](/edge-relay/reference/)). Saving the tag reloads the running
device, so a change takes effect on the next poll and nothing restarts by hand.
A re-discovery leaves a tag's list alone.

## Quality

Every reading carries `good`, `uncertain` or `bad`.

**Bad means the value is not known. It does not mean zero.** A driver that
cannot read a point still emits a reading, marked bad, because silence is
indistinguishable from a value that has not changed, and on a trend, the
difference between "the sensor reads 0" and "the sensor stopped answering" is the
difference between a process problem and an instrument problem.

Alarm evaluation holds its previous state on a bad reading rather than
evaluating it. A sensor that fails to zero would otherwise trip every low alarm
on the unit and look like a process event.
